label: The familiar cube returns along the walk
before: Enter along the coloured centre path. Confetti opens above it. You have not solved a puzzle yet. Stay a moment with the possibility that the room is pleased you arrived.
after:
Enter along the coloured centre path. Confetti opens above it. You have not solved a puzzle yet. Stay a moment with the possibility that the room is pleased you arrived.

The little wire cubes have returned, spaced along the middle of the walk. Walk into one. Its outline disappears and sparks rise from its place, drawing long coloured tails through the air. Keep walking. Another cube, another burst. For a moment, the celebration marks where you have been.

label: A note for later
before: They already share the room, even when the arch has no place for them. What would you have to change in the list, or in the rule that builds it, to give another colour a place in the arch?
after: They already share the room, even when the arch has no place for them. What would you have to change in the list, or in the rule that builds it, to give another colour a place in the arch?[^colour-boundaries]

label: A banner to walk beneath
before: Before leaving, choose the version you want to stand beneath. Let the confetti return. The same programmed event can be a reward for obedience or an invitation that asks nothing of you; here you can repeat it without passing a test.
after: Before leaving, choose the version you want to stand beneath. Let the confetti return. At the far end of the walk, two slender poles hold a rainbow banner above your head. You can pass beneath it whether you collected every cube or left them all. The same programmed event can be a reward for obedience or an invitation that asks nothing of you; here you can repeat the confetti without passing a test.

label: Footnote retained as a later line of inquiry
after: [^colour-boundaries]: A question for later: queer has no compulsory colour. A flag, a garment and a pastel wall do different work. We cannot assume that conservatives share a fear of pastels; we can ask when a colour becomes a threat to an order that wants its distinctions kept. In *Powers of Horror* (1982), Julia Kristeva connects abjection with disturbances of identity, system and order ([opening chapter, pp. 1–4](https://ieas-szeged.hu/downtherabbithole/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/Kristeva_Abjection.pdf)). This offers a way to question the policing of a boundary, without calling queer bodies abject. A future encounter could let us soften the bands or mix their colours towards white. These are different operations. A continuous control would still have limits; smoothness alone would not make it free.
